ai.definition: Smart grids are electrical power networks that use digital technology to monitor and manage the process of electricity being moved from suppliers to consumers.
ai.howItWorks: They integrate advanced sensors (such as smart meters), communication technologies, and computer processing to provide real-time data on energy usage, distribution, and system status. This enables utilities to optimize energy distribution, detect issues early, and respond more quickly to outages or other disruptions.
ai.problemSolved: Smart grids address the inefficiencies of traditional power grids by improving reliability, reducing energy losses, and facilitating better management of renewable energy sources.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves producing smart meters, sensors, communication devices, and integrating these with existing grid infrastructure. This includes customizing hardware for harsh outdoor environments and developing software to manage data flows and analytics.
ai.buildProcess: The build process starts with designing the system architecture, selecting appropriate technologies, and then assembling components such as sensors, communication devices, and control systems. Integration with existing power grid infrastructure is a critical step, followed by testing and commissioning.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include initial investment in new hardware and software, ongoing maintenance costs, and potential upgrades to existing infrastructure. Energy savings over time can offset these costs but require careful planning and implementation.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook for smart grids is positive as more utilities recognize the benefits of modernizing their systems. However, widespread adoption faces challenges such as high initial investment and regulatory hurdles.
ai.regulation: Regulations vary by region but generally require standards for data security, interoperability, and privacy protection. Governments often provide incentives to encourage deployment.
ai.risks: Risks include cybersecurity threats, integration difficulties with existing infrastructure, and the potential for high upfront costs deterring smaller utilities or developing countries.
ai.profitability: Profitability can be achieved through reduced operational costs, increased energy efficiency, and new revenue streams from demand response programs. However, these benefits may take time to materialize.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on enhancing cybersecurity measures, improving energy storage integration, and expanding the use of artificial intelligence for predictive maintenance and optimization.

glossary.def: A device that records electricity consumption in real-time and transmits this data to utility companies.
Measures taken to protect the integrity, confidentiality, and availability of smart grid systems from digital attacks.
The ability of different devices or systems to work together effectively without special effort on the part of users.

subsystems.name: Sensing and metering
subsystems.role: measures what is actually happening across the network, from substations to homes.
parts: phasor measurement units for time-synchronised readings

subsystems.name: Communications
subsystems.role: carries those measurements and control commands reliably and fast.
parts: cellular or radio mesh for meters and pole-top devices

subsystems.name: Control and automation software
subsystems.role: turns data into switching, voltage and dispatch decisions.

subsystems.name: Switchgear and power electronics
subsystems.role: the muscles that act on the network.
parts: static compensators and flexible AC transmission devices

subsystems.name: Distributed energy resources interface
subsystems.role: lets rooftop solar, batteries and electric vehicles help rather than hinder.

subsystems.name: Demand-side and market platform
subsystems.role: signals when to shift or cut consumption, and settles the payments.

subsystems.name: Cybersecurity and resilience layer
subsystems.role: protects a system that is now remotely controllable.
parts: intrusion monitoring and secure firmware updates

buildSteps.title: Map the network
buildSteps.detail: Record every feeder, transformer, switch and customer connection in a digital model, because you cannot control what you have not mapped.

buildSteps.title: Install smart meters
buildSteps.detail: Replace mechanical meters at customer premises with units that report consumption and voltage every 15–30 minutes.

buildSteps.title: Instrument the substations
buildSteps.detail: Fit current, voltage and temperature sensors, and remote-control relays to breakers and reclosers on poles and in substations.

buildSteps.title: Build the communications backbone
buildSteps.detail: Lay fibre to primary substations and use cellular or radio mesh for the many small devices that cannot justify a fibre link.

buildSteps.title: Deploy the control platforms
buildSteps.detail: Commission SCADA, distribution management and outage management systems, and link them to the field devices through standard protocols.

buildSteps.title: Automate switching and voltage
buildSteps.detail: Configure reclosers and tie switches to isolate faults and restore supply automatically, and coordinate capacitors and regulators to hold voltage in range.

buildSteps.title: Open the platform to flexible resources
buildSteps.detail: Apply grid codes (e.g. IEEE 1547) so inverters can ride through disturbances, provide reactive power and be curtailed by the operator when needed.

buildSteps.title: Run demand response and tariffs
buildSteps.detail: Recruit flexible loads — industry, heat pumps, chargers, batteries — into programmes that cut or shift demand at peak, with measurement and settlement to pay them.

buildSteps.title: Harden and operate
buildSteps.detail: Segment networks, monitor for intrusion, patch firmware, and keep forecasters and operators in the loop as renewable and electric-vehicle shares grow.

prerequisites.why: without a fast, reliable link to each device, monitoring and control are impossible.
smart meters and smart inverters must be cheap enough to fit by the million.
storage is what turns a signal into a physical change in supply and demand.
weather, load and price forecasts drive the scheduling decisions the grid acts on.
a remotely controllable grid is a target, and legacy equipment was never designed to be secure.

pathway.milestone: smart meters, remote switching and demand response at scale in many regions
pathway.unlocks: faster outage restoration and measurable peak-demand reduction.

pathway.milestone: active distribution management with high rooftop solar and battery penetration
pathway.unlocks: hosting far more local generation without rebuilding every feeder.

pathway.milestone: grid-forming inverters, dynamic line ratings and vehicle-to-grid charging
pathway.unlocks: using the network closer to its physical limits and using electric vehicles as storage.

pathway.milestone: wide-area, cross-border control with integrated flexibility markets
pathway.unlocks: reliable supply from a system dominated by variable renewables.
